data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), not probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' cannot be defined without invoking probabilistic assumptions about the distribution of truths.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the act of preferring a theory for future action implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past (the principle of induction).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own advice to engineers relies on an unstated inductive bridge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains improbable regardless of tests) and the rational basis for preferring one theory over another for practical application. The mechanism is 'critical preference': we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification because it has demonstrated higher content and resilience, making it the best available approximation to truth (verisimilitude) without implying it is probably true. This avoids induction by treating corroboration as a report of past performance, not a predictor of future success via uniformity of nature.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
